description: Error Spotting is a crucial component of English Grammar and Competitive Exams. It involves identifying grammatical, semantic, or structural mistakes in a given sentence.

sections.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
sections.description: The verb in a sentence must always agree with its main subject in number and person.

grammar_rules.structure: Subject 1 + (as well as / along with / together with / besides) + Subject 2 + Verb (according to Subject 1)
grammar_rules.explanation: When two subjects are joined by words like 'as well as', 'along with', or 'together with', the verb always agrees with the first subject.

grammar_rules.structure: (Either...or / Neither...nor / Not only...but also) + Subject 2 + Verb (according to Subject 2)
grammar_rules.explanation: In sentences joined by these correlative conjunctions, the verb always agrees with the nearest subject.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The captain along with his players are going to the ground.
examples.correct_or_usage: The captain along with his players is going to the ground.
examples.explanation: Because of 'along with', the verb must agree with the first subject 'captain' (Singular) and not 'players'.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Neither the teacher nor the students is present.
examples.correct_or_usage: Neither the teacher nor the students are present.
examples.explanation: The subject nearest to the verb is 'students' (Plural), so 'are' must be used.

exceptions.explanation: When a collective noun (like Jury, Committee, Team) acts as a single unit, it takes a singular verb. However, when there is a difference of opinion or division among the members, it takes a plural verb.
exceptions.example: The committee is unanimous on this issue. (Unit) | The committee are divided in their opinion. (Divided)

sections.title: Tense Consistency and Conditional Sentences
sections.description: Correct and logical use of tenses across different clauses of a sentence is essential.

key_concepts.explanation: Sentences that state a condition and its outcome. The tense in the 'If-clause' and the 'Main clause' follows specific fixed combinations.

grammar_rules.structure: Subject + V2 (Simple Past) + ... (yesterday / last year / in 2010)
grammar_rules.explanation: When a specific past time is mentioned in the sentence, the Simple Past Tense must be used, not the Present Perfect Tense.

grammar_rules.structure: If + Subject + V1 (Simple Present), Subject + will/shall + V1 (Simple Future)
grammar_rules.explanation: For a highly probable future event, the 'If-clause' uses the Present Tense, while the Main Clause uses the Future Tense.

examples.incorrect_or_context: I have completed my graduation in 2018.
examples.explanation: '2018' is a specific past time, so 'completed' (V2) is correct instead of 'have completed' (Present Perfect).

examples.incorrect_or_context: If I will reach early, I will call you.
examples.correct_or_usage: If I reach early, I will call you.
examples.explanation: In conditional sentences, the future tense ('will') is not used in the condition (If-clause).

sections.title: Nouns and Pronouns
sections.description: Errors related to the types of nouns (countable/uncountable) and the strict agreement of a pronoun with its antecedent.

key_concepts.explanation: Nouns that cannot be counted (e.g., information, luggage, poetry, scenery, machinery, furniture). We do not use 'a/an' before them, nor do we add 's/es' to make them plural.

grammar_rules.explanation: When the subject of a sentence is the indefinite pronoun 'One', the corresponding possessive pronoun must be 'one's', not 'his' or 'her'.

examples.incorrect_or_context: He gave me many useful informations.
examples.correct_or_usage: He gave me much useful information. (or 'a lot of useful information')
examples.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun; thus, it does not take an 's' and uses 'much' instead of 'many'.
The possessive case for the subject 'One' is 'one's', not 'his'.

exceptions.explanation: To denote quantity or numbers for uncountable nouns, we use specific partitive phrases instead of directly adding 's/es'.
exceptions.example: A piece of information, Two items of furniture, A loaf of bread.

sections.title: Prepositions and Conjunctions
sections.description: Evaluating the fixed and accurate usage of prepositions (showing relations) and conjunctions (connecting clauses).

grammar_rules.structure: Word ending in '-ior' (senior, junior, superior, inferior) + to + Object
grammar_rules.explanation: Comparative adjectives of Latin origin and the verb 'prefer' are followed by the preposition 'to' instead of the conjunction 'than'.

grammar_rules.structure: Although / Though + Subject + Verb, yet / comma (,) + Subject + Verb
grammar_rules.explanation: Sentences starting with 'Although' or 'Though' should not use 'but' in the second clause. Instead, they must be followed by 'yet' or simply a comma.

examples.incorrect_or_context: She is senior than me by three years.
examples.correct_or_usage: She is senior to me by three years.
examples.explanation: The word 'senior' is always followed by the preposition 'to', never by 'than'.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Although he is rich, but he is a miser.
examples.correct_or_usage: Although he is rich, yet he is a miser. (Or: Although he is rich, he is a miser.)

sections.title: Strategies for Error Spotting
sections.description: An effective, step-by-step approach to solving error spotting questions with speed and accuracy in exams.

strategies.title: Read the Sentence Completely
strategies.detail: Read the entire sentence without pausing to find errors immediately. Often, the natural reading flow helps identify awkward or incorrect structures.

strategies.title: Isolate Subject and Verb
strategies.detail: Mentally remove distracting prepositional phrases or modifiers. Identify the core subject and verify if the verb correctly agrees with it in number.

strategies.title: Verify Time and Tense
strategies.detail: Look for time indicator words (like yesterday, tomorrow, since). Check if the tense consistency across the sentence remains logical.

strategies.title: Look for Fixed Pairs
strategies.detail: If you spot correlative conjunctions like Not only, Neither, Either, Although, No sooner, immediately check if their corresponding paired words are used correctly.
